name: Logboat (dugout)
dateNote: Logboats are found on the Thames and in its tributaries, but the London-area finds (Erith Marshes, 1885; Bourne End, upriver, drawn 1872) are undated or dated only by period guess. None is known from the City, Southwark or Westminster reach, so the type is shown only from the start of the Bourne End period attribution (2350 BCE). The type stays in use elsewhere in Britain long after the Roman conquest; it is not shown here after the Roman period.
summary: A boat hollowed from a single oak trunk, paddled. The Bourne End logboat was 7.6 m long and 1 m wide, with an upturned pointed bow, a square stern and three carved ribs or seats.
uncertainty: Prehistoric boat finds in the greater Thames are very few. The form follows the Bourne End boat; no logboat is evidenced in this reach, so any shown here is illustrative.

name: Romano-Celtic sailing barge (Blackfriars 1 type)
dateNote: Blackfriars ship 1 is dendro-dated to about AD 150 and sank soon after. The same build is known from the 1st to about the 4th century in Britain and Gaul (Barland's Farm boat, c. 300).
summary: A flat-bottomed, keel-less ship of oak, frame-first, its flush-laid planks fixed to the frames with large iron nails turned over inside. Blackfriars 1 was about 16-17 m long and 6 m in beam, with sides over 2.5 m high, a single mast stepped about a third of the length from the bow, and a cargo of some 26 tons of Kentish ragstone from the Medway.
uncertainty: Length is given as 16-17 m (14 m survived). The rig is inferred from the mast step: a single square sail is the usual reconstruction. No steering gear survived; the quarter steering oar drawn here is conjecture. Probably one of many such stone barges supplying the city.

name: Roman river barge (New Guy's House type)
dateNote: The New Guy's House boat (found 1958 in a former creek in Southwark) was abandoned about AD 200.
summary: A smaller flat-bottomed river barge of the same Romano-Celtic build as Blackfriars 1 (iron spikes through planks and frames, turned over like staples), about 16 m by 4 m, working the creeks and the river.
uncertainty: Dimensions come from a secondary summary. Whether it carried a mast is not established in the sources read, so none is drawn; it is shown poled or rowed.

name: Sea-going merchant ship, Mediterranean build (County Hall type)
dateNote: The County Hall ship sank after 293 (coins of Carausius and Allectus in its bottom); Milne gives its construction as about AD 285. Sea-going ships brought the port's imports from the 1st century, but the County Hall ship is the only one of this build found at London.
summary: A keeled, carvel-built oak ship whose planks were edge-joined with tenons in the Mediterranean manner, built shell-first, probably decked, and propelled by sail. Marsden estimated 60-70 ft (18-21 m) long, 15-16 ft (4.6-4.9 m) in beam and at least 6 ft deep: the smallest class of Roman merchant ship. Its oak is northern European, so it was built in the north by a builder who knew the Mediterranean method.
uncertainty: One find, of the late 3rd century, stands for the sea-going ships of the whole Roman port. Rig (one mast, square sail) and paired quarter rudders follow Roman practice and are not preserved. Such ships probably moored mid-stream and were unloaded by smaller craft.

name: Small boat or ferry (Roman)
dateNote: A landing stage of about AD 70, possibly a ferry terminal, is the only hint; no small Roman boat has been found at London.
summary: Small rowing boats for ferrying and harbour work must have existed beside the quays. None has been found at London, so the form (a small flush-planked rowing boat) is a stand-in.
uncertainty: Entirely inferred: form, size and numbers are illustrative.

name: Clinker-built trading boat, oared (Graveney type)
dateNote: Lundenwic traded by ship from about 600 and was abandoned by the 880s. The nearest dated comparison, the Graveney boat from the Kent marshes, is dendro-dated to about AD 895 (radiocarbon: late 9th century). Sutton Hoo (620s) shows the clinker tradition already established.
summary: A double-ended clinker boat of overlapping oak strakes held with iron rivets. The Graveney boat was over 14 m long and under 3 m in beam, a probable sea-going trader possibly built in southern or eastern England. Bede calls Lundenwic a trading centre for many nations who visit it by land and sea.
uncertainty: No boat has been found at Lundenwic. The form is borrowed from Graveney; Graveney shows no sign of a mast and the use of sail on English boats before the 9th century is debated, so it is drawn oared, with a steering oar on the starboard quarter.

name: Small clinker boat (ferrying, fishing)
dateNote: Small boats are named in the Billingsgate tolls (c. 1000: a small ship one halfpenny; a fish boat); fish traps and net weights show fishing throughout. From the 16th century the passenger wherry is a distinct type; small clinker boats stay in use for fishing and work.
summary: An open rowing boat of a few metres, built clinker in the northern tradition, used for ferrying, fishing and errands.
uncertainty: No dated small boat from this reach was found in the sources read; size and form are generic for the tradition.

name: Scandinavian longship, small (Skuldelev 5 type)
dateNote: Skuldelev 5 was built about 1030; Danish fleets are on the Thames from the 9th century to Cnut's in 1016.
summary: A narrow clinker warship rowed and sailed: Skuldelev 5 is 17.3 m long, 2.5 m wide, with 26 oars, a crew of about 30 and a 46 m² square sail. Steered by a side rudder on the starboard quarter.
uncertainty: No longship has been found in the Thames; the form is from the Roskilde finds.

name: Scandinavian longship, large (Skuldelev 2 type)
dateNote: Skuldelev 2 was built near Dublin from timber felled in 1042.
summary: A large clinker warship: Skuldelev 2 is 29.3 m long and 3.8 m wide, with 60 oars and a crew of 65-70. Single square sail; side rudder.
uncertainty: No longship has been found in the Thames; the form is from the Roskilde finds, and a ship of this size at London in 1014 is conjecture.

name: Clinker cargo ship with side rudder (keel type)
dateNote: The Billingsgate tolls (c. 978-1016, perhaps later) distinguish a larger ship with a sail and the ships of Rouen. Side rudders are still drawn on English seals into the early 14th century (Winchelsea).
summary: A beamy, double-ended clinker trader with a single square sail and a few oars, steered by a side rudder. Skuldelev 3 (c. 1040) is 14 m long and 3.3 m wide with a 45 m² sail and room for 4.6 t of cargo.
uncertainty: Form from Scandinavian comparanda and seal depictions; no such ship has been excavated at London (reused clinker planking is common in London's medieval waterfronts).

name: Clinker ship with castles and stern rudder (seal type)
dateNote: The Ipswich seal (1200) is the earliest depiction of a stern-post rudder; stern castles appear on larger ships from the 13th century. Large clinker ships were still built in the mid 15th century (the Newport ship, c. 1450s, about 35 m).
summary: A double-ended clinker ship with raised fore and aft castles, a single mast and square sail, steered by a rudder hung on the sternpost: the ship of the English town seals.
uncertainty: Known from seals and comparanda, not from a London find; size is illustrative. The written 'hulk' of the period cannot be matched to a surviving hull, so it is not shown as a separate type.

name: Cog (Bremen cog type)
dateNote: Cologne's merchants had a hall at Dowgate from 1157 and the Hanse merchants formed one London community in the later 13th century. The oldest depiction identified as a cog is the Lübeck seal of 1223; the Bremen cog dates from the 1380s.
summary: A high-sided cargo ship with a flush-laid flat bottom, clinker sides and long straight stem and stern posts, a stern rudder, one mast with a square sail and, on larger ships, a stern castle. The Bremen cog is about 23.3 m long, 7.6 m in beam, with sides just over 4 m high.
uncertainty: No cog has been excavated at London; their presence follows from the Hanseatic trade, not from a named ship. Dimensions are the Bremen cog's.

name: Shout, clinker river barge (Blackfriars 3)
dateNote: Blackfriars ship 3 was built locally between 1380 and 1415 and sank towards the end of the 15th century; the shout is described as the popular 14th- and 15th-century river transporter.
summary: A clinker-built sailing river barge, 14.64 m long, 4.3 m wide and 0.88 m deep, found in the riverbed between Trig Lane and Blackfriars (above the bridge). Single mast, square sail.
uncertainty: The steering arrangement is not given in the sources read; a stern rudder is drawn, as is usual by this date. How often it lowered its mast to pass the bridge is not known.

name: Lighter (open cargo barge)
dateNote: Larger ships of the medieval port moored mid-stream and were discharged by lighter; Stow (1598) calls Queenhithe a harbour for boats, lighters and barges.
summary: An open, flat, unrigged cargo barge, moved with the tide and long sweeps, carrying goods between ships and the quays.
uncertainty: No lighter of this period was examined; size and form are generic. Earlier unloading craft surely existed but are not shown before 1300.

name: State or livery-company barge
dateNote: The Brewers' Company records of 1422 hold the earliest account of a water procession on the Lord Mayor's Day; John Norman's procession by barge is usually dated 1453. Tudor coronations and royal removals went by barge.
summary: A long ceremonial rowing barge with a canopied house aft, painted and gilded, rowed by watermen. Earlier royal rowbarges were typically 60-75 ft (18-23 m) long.
uncertainty: Form and decoration of 15th- and 16th-century barges are not known in detail; the house, paint and number of oars are illustrative.

name: Carrack (carvel, high castles)
dateNote: Carvel construction reaches England in the later 15th century; the Newport ship (1450s) is still clinker, the Mary Rose (1510-12) is carvel, and by 1545 ships built on the Thames were carvel-built.
summary: A carvel-built ship with high fore and aft castles over a low waist, three or four masts (square sails on fore and main, a lateen mizzen) and a stern rudder. The Mary Rose had a keel of about 32 m.
uncertainty: Merchant carracks in the Pool were smaller than the Mary Rose; the size, castles and rig drawn are a generic reconstruction from the Mary Rose and contemporary pictures.

name: Hoy (single-masted coaster)
dateNote: A 'hoye of Dorderycht' is named in a Paston letter of 1495; hoys carried goods and passengers in the estuary and to ships in the Thames.
summary: A small one-masted coastal sailing vessel of the estuary and the Low Countries trade.
uncertainty: Size, build and sail plan before 1625 are not established in the sources read (the spritsail often drawn is not verified); the sail is shown brailed up to the mast.

name: Western barge (upriver cargo barge)
dateNote: Barges are named with lighters at Queenhithe in the 15th and 16th centuries (Stow, 1598), the market there having suffered when the drawbridge was no longer raised for larger vessels.
summary: A large, flat, open cargo barge working the river above the bridge, with a single mast and square sail; on the upper river such barges were also towed.
uncertainty: Form and size are reconstructed from the earlier shout (Blackfriars 3) and are not verified for this period.

name: Thames wherry
dateNote: The earliest record of Thames watermen is the fare statute of 1514; the Act of 1555 that created the Company of Watermen set a wherry at 22½ ft by 4½ ft amidships. Stow (1598) counts above 2,000 wherries and other small boats, setting at least 3,000 watermen to work.
summary: London's water taxi: a light, sharp-bowed clinker rowing boat about 6.9 m by 1.4 m, rowed by one or two watermen and carrying up to five passengers, above and below the bridge.
uncertainty: No wherry of this date survives; the form follows the statute dimensions and later pictures.

name: Tilt-boat (Gravesend long ferry)
dateNote: Ferries ran between Gravesend and Billingsgate (the long ferry) from the 13th century; boats with a tilt are associated with it from the mid 16th century, and Gravesend's boats were regulated from 1562 after complaints of badly built and overloaded vessels.
summary: A larger passenger rowing boat with a tilt (an awning) over the open well, plying between Billingsgate and Gravesend below the bridge.
uncertainty: The first date for a tilt-boat and its size before 1625 are not verified in the sources read; the earliest model seen dates from about 1650.

name: Armed merchant ship (Gresham ship type)
dateNote: The Gresham ship, lost in the Thames estuary, was built of English oak felled in or soon after 1574.
summary: A carvel-built, armed merchantman with gunports, about 24.5 m overall on a 19 m keel, 7.4 m in beam with a hold 3.4 m deep: a size matching many London ships of the day. Three masts (square sails on fore and main, a lateen mizzen), low castles in the galleon manner, a beakhead and a stern rudder.
uncertainty: The hull is the Gresham ship's; its rig did not survive and follows the general form of later 16th-century English ships.
